t: Learning under trees in the era of AI: The paradox of education in Mozambique

p.i: AI could help bridge educational inequality in a country where thousands of students still learn outdoors

The

p.t: overwhelming majority of the Mozambican population

p: speaks a Bantu language most frequently at home (81.7 percent), and a portion cannot speak Portuguese at all (41.9 percent), though it is the sole official language of the country due to its colonial history. Despite this, the media, official government communications, and healthcare institutions continue to privilege Portuguese to the detriment of Bantu languages — the languages of the masses — which, activists argue, constitutes a form of social exclusion. Emerging initiatives, however, show that it is possible to bridge this gap with the aid of technology.
, for instance, tech startups are developing AI solutions tailored to African languages.

Offline tools, pre-loaded content, and digital pedagogical assistants are some of the possible solutions to address the deficiencies and limitations of Mozambique’s education system. While the government

p.t: does not yet have specific policies

p: to integrate AI tools in schools, advocates say the state could play a central role in integrating technology into the daily lives of students and teachers. This also involves investing in teacher training; ensuring basic infrastructure; facilitating energy access; and strengthening partnerships with universities, startups, and international organizations.

Talking about artificial intelligence in outdoor classrooms may seem contradictory at first glance, but it is precisely in these contexts that technology needs to be considered creatively and responsibly, not as a replacement for the essential, but as a strategic complement.

The priority remains clear: Building schools, training teachers, and ensuring access to basic materials. The question is how to integrate developed technology without creating profound inequalities, respecting local contexts, and placing the student and teacher at the center of decision-making. In a country where learning still takes place under trees, the future of education will depend not only on the technology available, but also on the political and social choices that define who has access to knowledge and under what conditions.
